The standard permits any implementation-defined impact, including termination of the whole process, so a standalone program cannot distinguish a conforming impact from a violation of the implementation's documentation.

No portable C#1 source hook can deterministically inject an asynchronous exception precisely between successful Monitor.Enter and entry into the old try. Ordinary lock/body/exception controls agree at both levels and do not observe that boundary; same-thread TryEnter is reentrant and is not release evidence. IL spelling or hosted timing stress would impose an unrequired representation or timing oracle.

ed1-15.13-015: 15.13 states the rule, that the finally disposes of the resource and only a null resource skips Dispose (PDF p. 215 lines 8-10), and its 'precisely equivalent' code (lines 11-22) cannot be literal for every resource the clause admits: for a plain disposable struct, which 15.13 expressly allows (PDF p. 214 lines 45-46, PDF p. 215 lines 1-4), r1 != null is a compile-time error (PDF p. 181 lines 23-26), and for a class with a user-defined != the literal code would skip a non-null resource against lines 8-10. On this reading the observable behavior matches the 7th edition and csc (BODY:1:0), and the one remaining difference, the 7th edition's ban on boxing a value resource (PDF p. 362), cannot be observed because nothing reads the resource after Dispose. ed1-15.13-017: The multiple-resource text (PDF p. 215 lines 23-49) only repeats the single-resource finally for each resource, so the same whole-text reading applies (PDF p. 215 lines 8-10, PDF p. 181 lines 23-26) and it shares -015's semantics and any test; the retained facets (nested equivalence, acquisition order, reverse disposal) match the 7th edition 13.14. The residual no-boxing difference is unobservable, as for -015.
